example: Compare an intact phospholipid bilayer with the same membrane after an ion channel opens. The intact bilayer blocks water-soluble ions; the open channel supplies a selective crossing path.

en.title: The Cell Membrane as an Electrical Boundary
en.learning_objective: Explain how a phospholipid bilayer separates charge while membrane proteins control ion passage.
en.simple_explanation: A neuronal membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with watery fluid on both sides. Its nonpolar interior blocks water-soluble ions from crossing directly. Because ions carry charge, restricting their movement allows the two sides to maintain different ion distributions and electrical conditions.
en.how_it_works: The bilayer creates the barrier. Membrane-spanning channel proteins create pores through it, often selecting particular ions by pore diameter and chemical lining. Gated channels can open or close. An open channel permits passage, but net ion movement still requires a driving force such as a concentration difference or electrical field. Pumps use ATP to transport selected ions and help maintain unequal distributions.
en.visual:
outside: water + ions
──────── channel ────────
  nonpolar bilayer barrier
───────────┬─────────────
inside: water + ions
en.use_case: To predict whether an ion can affect neuronal voltage, first ask whether the membrane provides a channel for that ion; then ask what force would drive it through.
en.expected_result: With no suitable open channel, the bilayer restricts ion crossing. Opening a suitable channel creates a path, although direction and net flow depend on the forces acting on the ion.
en.what_to_notice: A membrane can act as an electrical boundary because it separates mobile charges selectively, not because it is an absolute wall. Permeability and driving force answer different questions.
en.common_mistake: Assuming that opening an ion channel automatically determines the direction of ion flow.
en.practical_tip: Use a two-step check: access—Is a suitable channel open? Drive—What concentration or electrical force acts on the ion?
en.question: Why can a neuronal membrane maintain electrical differences across it?
en.answer: Its phospholipid bilayer blocks direct ion passage, while selective channels and pumps regulate when and how charged ions cross.

review_items.question: What property of the phospholipid bilayer makes it an electrical boundary?
review_items.answer: Its nonpolar interior blocks water-soluble ions, allowing charge and ion distributions to differ across the membrane.

review_items.question: How does an ion channel change the boundary without removing it?
review_items.answer: A membrane-spanning protein forms a selective pore, giving certain ions a controlled path through the bilayer.

review_items.question: A Na+ channel opens, but Na+ concentrations and electrical conditions are equal on both sides. Why may there be no net Na+ movement?
review_items.answer: The channel provides access, but equal conditions supply no net concentration or electrical driving force.

active_exercise.instruction: Draw two side-by-side membrane cross-sections: A, an intact phospholipid bilayer with Na+ blocked; B, the same bilayer with an open Na+ channel. Add arrows showing no crossing in A and possible crossing in B. Under B, write: “path present; direction requires driving force.”
